title: Naming, lived
hook: the family gathers, the Granth is opened, the name begins with the hukam's letter
tomorrow: why does the code say a new mother needn't wait a set number of days?

segments.voice: Yesterday a child arrived, and the family gave thanks with Japji and Ardas: a new life. Now that new life needs something everyone will call out for years.

A new baby in the family group chat goes the same way every time: the photo, a wall of hearts, and then one question from every aunt at once. What's her name? Simran's Bhua Preet has been dodging it for days. Now it's Sunday, and the whole family is sitting on the gurdwara floor. The karah prashad is covered and waiting. Hymns of thanks have been sung, and Ardas said. Bhua Preet holds the baby, and the granthi opens the Guru Granth Sahib at random. Simran's dad, Harjit, leans so far forward he almost tips over. Because whatever sound starts the hymn on that page, the baby's name will start with it.
screen: `WHAT'S HER NAME?` → `SUNDAY, ON THE GURDWARA FLOOR.` → `THE GRANTH OPENED AT RANDOM.` → `THE FIRST SOUND DECIDES.`

segments.voice: This is the naming the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, describes. Once the mother is able, the family comes to the gurdwara with karah prashad. Hymns of thanks are sung, and the code names one by Guru Arjan on ang 396 that says, in paraphrase, the True Guru has sent this child. Then the Granth is opened, a hymn is read, and the granthi proposes a name beginning with the first letter of that hymn. A boy's name takes Singh. A girl's takes Kaur. The granthi reads. The first letter is sassa. Bhua had a list of names on her phone, and not one starts with sassa. Then Bebe Jaswant, Simran's grandmother, says one word: Sehaj. Calm, steady ease, a word from Gurbani. The sangat agrees. Sehaj Kaur. Here's the part worth telling a friend tonight. In Punjabi, naam means a name. In Gurbani, the same word, Naam, means the Name, God's presence, remembered. So a Sikh child's name begins inside the Name: its first sound is borrowed from the Guru's page. The parents still choose. The Guru picks where they start. Families keep the custom in their own ways, and the code gives the shape.
screen: `THE CODE: THANKS, THEN THE GRANTH.` · `THE FIRST LETTER OF THE HYMN.` · `SINGH OR KAUR.` · `NAAM: A NAME, AND THE NAME.` · then, large: `A NAME FROM THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write your own name by hand, slowly, the way you'd write it for a teacher on the first day. Then sit with what you know about it: who chose it, and why. If you don't know, let that question be the sit.
Naming. In a Sikh family, a name whose first sound comes from the hukam, the Guru's word opened at random.
Keep this one: a name from the guru, starting on the Guru's page. Welcome, Sehaj Kaur.
